hook: The Inca ruler who "shook the earth", built an empire and Machu Picchu.

pages.x: Cusi Yupanqui was a younger son of Viracocha, ruler of the small Inca kingdom around Cusco, high in the Andes. He was not meant to rule.

Around 1438 the powerful Chanka people attacked Cusco. The old king and his heir fled; Cusi Yupanqui stayed and defended the city. Legend says the very stones of the field rose up as warriors to fight for him. He won, took the throne and a new name: Pachacuti, "he who shakes the earth".
With his son Topa Inca, Pachacuti conquered much of the Andes, turning a small kingdom into Tawantinsuyu, "the four parts together", the largest empire in the Americas.

He rebuilt Cusco in stone, perhaps in the shape of a puma, with the fortress of Sacsayhuaman as its head, and a Temple of the Sun whose walls were covered in gold. Inca stones fit so tightly that a knife blade cannot slip between them.

High on a mountain ridge he built an estate of granite palaces, temples and terraces: Machu Picchu. The Spanish never found it. The world heard of it in 1911, when local farmers led the American explorer Hiram Bingham there.
He organised roads that grew to about 40,000 km, relay runners, storehouses, and records kept on quipus, strings tied with knots.
pages.fx: Messages could cross the empire at 240 km a day, and the stored food fed armies, and the hungry in bad years.

pages.x: Pachacuti turned a small Andean kingdom into the greatest empire of the Americas, with roads, cities and Machu Picchu. Peruvians honour him as one of the founders of their nation.
pts: Rebuilt Cusco as a city of stone
